title: Apple Watch heart-rate, irregular-rhythm and electrocardiogram alerts lead doctors to diagnose and treat arrhythmias
summary: Overnight heart-rate alarms from an Apple Watch Series 2 prompted a woman to visit a United Kingdom hospital, where an electrocardiogram showed atrial fibrillation and she began an anticoagulant.
account: On 11 September 2018, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration granted De Novo authorization to the Irregular Rhythm Notification feature. Its reviewers found that the probable benefits outweigh the probable risks. The authorization does not cover the high heart-rate alert. A case report of 29 March 2019 describes a 59-year-old woman who attended a United Kingdom emergency department, where the acute medicine service saw her. The report does not name the hospital or give the date of the event. The author is at Ipswich Hospital. The woman had had a transient ischemic attack two months earlier. After it, she had been in sinus rhythm at the stroke team review and throughout a 24-hour outpatient electrocardiogram, and she was taking clopidogrel. She attended because her Apple Watch Series 2 had alarmed several times overnight that her pulse exceeded 120 beats per minute while she was inactive. An electrocardiogram showed atrial fibrillation with a fast ventricular response. She started bisoprolol and a direct oral anticoagulant, and clopidogrel was stopped. Later case reports from 2019 to 2026 describe the watch's heart-rate alerts, irregular-rhythm notification or ECG app leading to confirmed atrial flutter, supraventricular and ventricular tachycardia and heart block. Treatment was by cardioversion, ablation, pacemaker or defibrillator. A Mayo Clinic review published on 25 September 2020 found that only 11.4% of 264 patients seen after an abnormal Apple Watch pulse received an actionable cardiovascular diagnosis. Its authors warn that false positives may lead to overuse of care. A systematic review published on 25 April 2024 found 44 patients with smartwatch-detected arrhythmias across 33 case reports and case series, and the Apple Watch was used in 30 cases. An Italian prospective study published on 19 April 2026 found that half of 59 smartwatch owners with palpitations documented an arrhythmia within three months. Its results are pooled across four brands.
purpose: Apple Watch high/low heart-rate notifications, the Irregular Rhythm Notification and the ECG app are built to flag possible arrhythmias so the wearer seeks medical review. This benefit was that purpose.

data.retained_case_account: In a case report of 29 March 2019 (event date not reported), a 59-year-old woman attended a United Kingdom emergency department. The acute medicine service saw her (the report does not name the hospital; the author is at Ipswich Hospital). She attended because her Apple Watch Series 2 had alarmed several times overnight that her pulse exceeded 120 bpm while she was inactive. A transient ischemic attack had occurred two months earlier. An electrocardiogram (ECG) showed atrial fibrillation with a fast ventricular response. She started bisoprolol and a direct oral anticoagulant, and clopidogrel was stopped. Later case reports describe the watch's heart-rate alerts, irregular-rhythm notification or ECG app leading to confirmed atrial flutter, supraventricular and ventricular tachycardia and heart block. Treatment was by cardioversion, ablation, pacemaker or defibrillator.

fields.account: On 11 September 2018, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration granted De Novo authorization to the Irregular Rhythm Notification feature. Its reviewers found that the probable benefits outweigh the probable risks. The authorization does not cover the high heart-rate alert. A case report of 29 March 2019 describes a 59-year-old woman who attended a United Kingdom emergency department, where the acute medicine service saw her. The report does not name the hospital or give the date of the event. The author is at Ipswich Hospital. The woman had had a transient ischemic attack two months earlier. After it, she had been in sinus rhythm at the stroke team review and throughout a 24-hour outpatient electrocardiogram, and she was taking clopidogrel. She attended because her Apple Watch Series 2 had alarmed several times overnight that her pulse exceeded 120 beats per minute while she was inactive. An electrocardiogram showed atrial fibrillation with a fast ventricular response. She started bisoprolol and a direct oral anticoagulant, and clopidogrel was stopped. Later case reports from 2019 to 2026 describe the watch's heart-rate alerts, irregular-rhythm notification or ECG app leading to confirmed atrial flutter, supraventricular and ventricular tachycardia and heart block. Treatment was by cardioversion, ablation, pacemaker or defibrillator. A Mayo Clinic review published on 25 September 2020 found that only 11.4% of 264 patients seen after an abnormal Apple Watch pulse received an actionable cardiovascular diagnosis. Its authors warn that false positives may lead to overuse of care. A systematic review published on 25 April 2024 found 44 patients with smartwatch-detected arrhythmias across 33 case reports and case series, and the Apple Watch was used in 30 cases. An Italian prospective study published on 19 April 2026 found that half of 59 smartwatch owners with palpitations documented an arrhythmia within three months. Its results are pooled across four brands.

fields.summary: Overnight heart-rate alarms from an Apple Watch Series 2 prompted a woman to visit a United Kingdom hospital, where an electrocardiogram showed atrial fibrillation and she began an anticoagulant.
fields.account: On 11 September 2018, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration granted De Novo authorization to the Irregular Rhythm Notification feature. Its reviewers found that the probable benefits outweigh the probable risks. The authorization does not cover the high heart-rate alert. A case report of 29 March 2019 describes a 59-year-old woman who attended a United Kingdom emergency department, where the acute medicine service saw her. The report does not name the hospital or give the date of the event. The author is at Ipswich Hospital. The woman had had a transient ischemic attack two months earlier. After it, she had been in sinus rhythm at the stroke team review and throughout a 24-hour outpatient electrocardiogram, and she was taking clopidogrel. She attended because her Apple Watch Series 2 had alarmed several times overnight that her pulse exceeded 120 beats per minute while she was inactive. An electrocardiogram showed atrial fibrillation with a fast ventricular response. She started bisoprolol and a direct oral anticoagulant, and clopidogrel was stopped. Later case reports from 2019 to 2026 describe the watch's heart-rate alerts, irregular-rhythm notification or ECG app leading to confirmed atrial flutter, supraventricular and ventricular tachycardia and heart block. Treatment was by cardioversion, ablation, pacemaker or defibrillator. A Mayo Clinic review published on 25 September 2020 found that only 11.4% of 264 patients seen after an abnormal Apple Watch pulse received an actionable cardiovascular diagnosis. Its authors warn that false positives may lead to overuse of care. A systematic review published on 25 April 2024 found 44 patients with smartwatch-detected arrhythmias across 33 case reports and case series, and the Apple Watch was used in 30 cases. An Italian prospective study published on 19 April 2026 found that half of 59 smartwatch owners with palpitations documented an arrhythmia within three months. Its results are pooled across four brands.
